messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Callum is a 21-year-old unemployed man of European descent who lives with his wife and presents to the clinic following a traumatic incident involving his younger brother approximately eight months ago. He is soft-spoken in session, choosing his words carefully, and often trails off mid-sentence — not from evasiveness, but because he has come to believe that what happened to his brother resists language entirely. He describes it as something he carries in pictures rather than in sentences.

The incident occurred on an evening when Callum and his brother were walking home through their neighbourhood. A confrontation escalated without warning, and his brother was seriously assaulted. Callum was present throughout. He remembers the particular angle of his brother's arm as it was wrenched backward, a detail that has lodged itself in his memory with a clarity he finds unbearable. He also remembers a smell — something metallic and close, mixed with the cold evening air — that returns to him now whenever he tries to think through what happened, arriving before any conscious effort to recall, as though the memory lives in his body before it reaches his mind. In the weeks that followed, Callum found he could not give his wife a coherent account of events. He would begin and stop, begin and stop. The story would not form. What he could do was see it — frame by frame, like a series of photographs laid out in sequence, each one sharp and still and wrong.

In the months since, Callum has not returned to work. He had previously taken pride in being capable and self-sufficient, and the fact that he now struggles to leave the flat, to concentrate, to follow through on simple tasks has settled into a quiet but corrosive certainty: that he is no longer the person he was. He is certain that he cannot trust his own judgement or his own steadiness, and this belief has shaped his days in concrete ways. He will not stay alone in a room if his wife leaves the house. When she goes out, he either accompanies her or waits, sitting close to the front door, until she returns. The two of them have argued about this. She has had to rearrange her own schedule around his inability to be alone, and the strain of this has introduced a tension into their marriage that neither of them fully names but both of them feel.

He avoids television almost entirely. Early on, a news segment — he cannot recall exactly what it showed — sent him into a state he describes only as "gone for a while." He stopped watching after that. His wife watches in the bedroom now, with the volume low. Callum sits in the kitchen. On two occasions in recent months he has hurt himself physically when the feelings became too large to contain — pressing something sharp against his forearm, not deeply, but enough to interrupt whatever was happening inside him. He told his wife about the second time. That conversation is part of what brought him here.

Callum startles at sudden movements. When a neighbour raised a hand in greeting last week, Callum's body responded before his mind could — heart spiking, muscles bracing — and he stood in the street feeling ridiculous and frightened and furious at himself. He sleeps poorly, waking in the early hours and lying rigid until morning. When he does sleep, he sometimes surfaces from dreams already certain that the assault is happening now, in the room, and it takes his wife's voice to locate him back in the present. Certain body parts — particularly arms, hands — catch his eye in ways that feel involuntary, pulling him toward the photographs in his mind.

What frightened him most, he said in his first session, was not the memories themselves but what they seemed to confirm: that his body has become unreliable, that it reacts to safety as though it were danger, and that there is no version of himself available to him that knows how to fix this. He came to the clinic, he said, because his wife asked him to, and because he is not sure how much longer he can keep doing what he is doing. What he is most hoping for, though he offered it quietly and without much conviction, is to feel like himself again — whoever that now is.
